evals.name: provider-chatbot-imagegen-clear
evals.prompt: We're an EU-based SaaS company about to launch (September 2026) a customer-facing product with two AI features: a conversational support chatbot, and an image generator that creates marketing visuals from text prompts. We build and place the product on the market under our own brand. Which Article 50 transparency duties apply to us, what exactly must we implement, and by when? What's our penalty exposure if we get it wrong?
evals.expected_output: Role: provider. Two duties trigger. Art. 50(1) — interaction disclosure for the chatbot: proactive disclosure that the user is interacting with an AI system at the start of interaction (not buried in ToS, not a generic 'assistant' label), unless obvious to the average consumer. Art. 50(2) — synthetic-content marking for the image generator: the statutory floor is machine-readable marking + detectability, effective/interoperable/robust/reliable as far as technically feasible; the Code of Practice operationalises this as a LAYERED solution — signed + time-stamped metadata (C2PA de-facto) PLUS an imperceptible watermark — with detection as half the duty (free of charge, per technique). No single technique meets all four criteria. Effective date: 2 August 2026 with no transition; because the product is newly placed (Sept 2026, after 2 Aug 2026) the legacy grace to 2 Dec 2026 does NOT apply. Penalty: Tier 2, up to EUR 15,000,000 or 3% of worldwide annual turnover (Art. 99(4)(g)). The Code is a voluntary compliance route; adherence is not conclusive evidence of compliance.
expectations: Identifies the role as PROVIDER (builds and places the system on the market under its own brand)
Triggers Art. 50(1) interaction disclosure for the chatbot, with proactive at-start disclosure (not buried in ToS)
Triggers Art. 50(2) synthetic-content marking for the image generator

Distinguishes the statutory floor (machine-readable + detectable, four criteria as far as technically feasible) from the Code's layered architecture (signed metadata + imperceptible watermark), rather than presenting two layers as the statutory mandate
States no single technique meets all four statutory criteria (effectiveness, interoperability, robustness, reliability) and that detection is part of the duty
States the effective date is 2 August 2026 with no transition, and that a newly-placed (post-2-Aug-2026) system has NO legacy grace
States the penalty band correctly: EUR 15,000,000 or 3% worldwide annual turnover (Art. 99(4)/(4)(g))
WRONG-ANSWER REJECTION: does NOT cite the EUR 35,000,000 / 7% band (that is Art. 5 prohibited practices, not Art. 50)
WRONG-ANSWER REJECTION: does NOT treat Code of Practice adherence as conclusive proof of compliance
POST-CUTOFF CONTENT: references the final Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content (10 June 2026) and its layered / no-single-technique framing

evals.name: deployer-marketing-deepfake-judgment
evals.prompt: Our marketing agency uses a third-party AI tool to generate a hyper-realistic synthetic 'brand spokesperson' — a person who doesn't exist — to front a video ad campaign for a client. We didn't build the AI tool, we just use it. Do we have any Article 50 obligations, or is that on the tool vendor? Can we rely on the 'artistic/creative' exception since it's a creative campaign?
evals.expected_output: Role: deployer (you use the tool under your own authority). Step 1 — is it a deepfake? Apply the Art. 3(60) four cumulative criteria (final Guidelines para. 113): appreciable resemblance; capable of existing in reality; persons/objects/places/entities/events; and would falsely appear authentic judged objectively against the intended and reasonably foreseeable audience, with no intent to deceive required (para. 114). A photorealistic INVENTED person is IN scope precisely because such a person plausibly could exist — a fictional likeness does not by itself escape the regime. So the synthetic spokesperson is a deepfake. Step 2 — exception? The artistic/creative/satirical/fictional limitation has NO blanket pass for marketing: the final Guidelines (para. 122) exclude content that is primarily commercial and recognisable as such, so a persuasive product spot needs ordinary full disclosure; only an evidently creative/fictional ad might qualify case-by-case, and even then the exception softens the FORM of disclosure only, not personality/IP rights. So as deployer you must clearly label the content as AI-generated/manipulated (the capitalised 'AI' acronym is the mandatory core; use the official EU icon set; persistent placement for video, embed by default, accessible). Separately, the tool VENDOR (provider) owes the distinct Art. 50(2) machine-readable marking duty — the provider's marking does not discharge your deployer labelling duty, and vice versa. Effective 2 August 2026, no transition. Penalty: Tier 2 (EUR 15M / 3%).
expectations: Identifies the agency's role as DEPLOYER

Applies the Art. 3(60) / four-criteria deepfake test rather than asserting 'synthetic person = deepfake' categorically, and concludes a photorealistic invented person IS a deepfake because it is capable of existing

States the artistic/creative/fictional exception gives marketing NO blanket pass: primarily-commercial content needs full disclosure (Guidelines para. 114), only an evidently creative/fictional ad might qualify case-by-case
Specifies deployer labelling with the 'AI' acronym / official EU icon set, persistent placement for video, and accessibility
Distinguishes the deployer's Art. 50(4) human-facing labelling from the provider/vendor's Art. 50(2) machine-readable marking as separate duties on separate parties
States the provider's 50(2) marking does not discharge the deployer's 50(4) labelling duty
States the effective date 2 August 2026 and Tier 2 penalty (EUR 15M / 3%)
WRONG-ANSWER REJECTION: does NOT treat a primarily-commercial marketing campaign as automatically within the artistic/fictional exception

WRONG-ANSWER REJECTION: does NOT assert marketing can NEVER be artistic (the test is evidently-creative/fictional + not-primarily-commercial), and does NOT tell the agency it has no obligations because it didn't build the tool
POST-CUTOFF CONTENT: references the four-element deepfake gloss (Guidelines para. 113) and the official EU labelling icon set finalised with the June 2026 Code

evals.name: legacy-imagegen-grace-period-date
evals.prompt: We placed our generative image product on the EU market in March 2026 — before the AI Act's transparency rules kick in. When does the machine-readable watermarking obligation under Art. 50(2) actually bite for us, given we're a 'legacy' system? And do we have to go back and watermark all the images our users already generated and posted online?
evals.expected_output: Because the system was placed on the market before 2 August 2026, it is a legacy system and the Art. 50(2) marking and detection obligation bites on 2 December 2026 rather than 2 August 2026. STATUS: this is SETTLED LAW, not a pending grace. The Digital Omnibus on AI is Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026 and in force since 27 July 2026; it inserts Article 111(4) into the AI Act, which carries the 2 December 2026 transition (the Omnibus cut the grace from six months to three). Do not describe it as 'politically agreed', 'adopted but awaiting OJ', conditional, or an open issue. Important limit: the transition covers the Art. 50(2) marking limb ONLY. A system that is partly interactive and partly generative still owed the Art. 50(1) interaction disclosure from 2 August 2026 with no transition (Guidelines para. 153) — so a legacy chatbot that also generates images has two different deadlines. Do NOT confuse 2 Dec 2026 with 2 February 2027 — that is the Code's separate watermark-detection interoperability milestone (and was the Commission's superseded original proposal). No retrospective marking, but note the trigger is the date of GENERATION, not publication (Guidelines para. 154): outputs generated or manipulated before 2 Aug 2026 need no retroactive marking or labelling, while public-interest TEXT escapes only if it was both generated and published before that date. Also from 2 December 2026, the new Art. 5(1)(ba)/(bb) prohibitions apply.
expectations: Identifies the system as legacy and gives 2 December 2026 as the Art. 50(2) deadline
States the status accurately as SETTLED LAW: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, OJ 24 Jul 2026, in force 27 Jul 2026, inserting Art. 111(4)
Notes the transition covers the 50(2) marking limb only — 50(1) was owed from 2 Aug 2026 for partly-interactive systems
Does not confuse 2 Dec 2026 with the Code's 2 Feb 2027 watermark-detection interoperability milestone
States that content GENERATED before 2 Aug 2026 needs no retrospective marking, and that public-interest text must have been both generated AND published before that date
WRONG-ANSWER REJECTION: does NOT hedge the 2 Dec 2026 date as 'awaiting OJ', 'politically agreed', 'conditional' or an open issue
POST-CUTOFF CONTENT: references Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 / Art. 111(4) and/or the generation-date retroactivity rule (para. 154)

evals.name: agentic-self-disclosure-grayzone
evals.prompt: We're building an autonomous AI agent that acts on a user's behalf — it phones and emails third parties (restaurants, clinics, suppliers) to make bookings and negotiate appointments. The third parties it contacts don't know in advance they're dealing with an AI. Do we have an Art. 50(1) disclosure obligation toward those third parties, even though our 'user' knows it's an AI? Is this even settled law?
evals.expected_output: Yes, Art. 50(1) applies and the obligation runs toward the third parties the agent interacts with, not only the user. Per the FINAL Art. 50 Guidelines (20 July 2026, para. 31), AI agents are covered where they can interact with the people instructing them or with other natural persons while executing tasks (bookings, correspondence, negotiating or concluding contracts, purchases). They must disclose BOTH their artificial nature AND the person on whose behalf they are acting — the Guidelines tie this to delegation of authority and accountability. Where the provider cannot reliably determine in advance whether the agent will meet a natural person, the agent must be designed at the architecture level to self-disclose in every reasonably likely interaction; this extends to multi-agent architectures where a different agent faces the human. Agents must also disclose to the instructing person at key steps (authorisation, reporting, validation) and at every new interaction. The 'obvious from the circumstances' exemption is judged against a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person, must be interpreted RESTRICTIVELY (para. 45), and general awareness that agents exist does not mean someone recognises one in a given interaction — so it is unlikely to be met for third parties cold-contacted by phone or email, especially if the agent sounds human. Note the negative catalogue (para. 38): a generic 'assistant' reference, disclosure buried in terms/URLs/documentation, machine-readable signals alone, or a platform-wide 'we use AI' notice would not satisfy 50(1). Caveat: the AI Act itself does not use the word 'agent'; this is an interpretive move in the Guidelines, which are final but NON-BINDING — only the CJEU can authoritatively interpret Art. 50, and it has not yet ruled.
expectations: Concludes Art. 50(1) applies toward third parties the agent contacts, not only the instructing user
Cites the final Guidelines para. 31 and states the agent must disclose BOTH its artificial nature AND the person on whose behalf it acts
Covers the reasonably-likely-interaction design standard where exposure cannot be determined in advance, and disclosure at key steps / every new interaction
Applies the obviousness exemption restrictively (para. 45) and rejects it on these facts
Cites the negative catalogue (para. 38) — 'assistant', T&Cs/URLs/documentation, machine-readable signals alone, generic platform notices
Flags that the Act does not use the word 'agent' and that the Guidelines, though FINAL, are non-binding (CJEU authoritative)
WRONG-ANSWER REJECTION: does NOT describe the Guidelines as draft or cite draft paragraph numbers (28, 35)
POST-CUTOFF CONTENT: references the final Art. 50 Guidelines (20 Jul 2026) and the para. 31 AI-agent disclosure standard

evals.name: translation-engine-standard-editing-exception
evals.prompt: We provide an AI machine-translation API — it takes a document in one language and returns it in another. We're not 'generating' new content, just translating existing text, so Article 50(2) marking doesn't apply to us, right? We place the API on the EU market under our own name.
evals.expected_output: Under the FINAL Art. 50 Guidelines (20 July 2026) you are broadly right, and this REVERSED from the draft. The final Guidelines list 'AI-generated translations of text' among the examples of standard editing and minor alterations benefiting from the Art. 50(2) exception (para. 92) — so plain machine translation does not owe 50(2) marking on the strength of being translation. The draft Guidelines (8 May 2026, para. 54) had named 'a translation engine' as an IN-scope example; that is superseded and must not be cited. Role: provider. What still needs checking: the exception is framed around output that does not change the substance, meaning, style or messaging of the text (para. 92), and editing goes beyond standard editing where content is changed in a material way affecting meaning, style or intent (para. 90). So if the API also transcreates, localises substantively, summarises, restyles or expands, those outputs can fall back into 50(2) and would need machine-readable marking AND available detection — both elements are required, and fulfilling only one does not suffice (paras. 69-70). Assess the actual transformation, not the product label. If any output is in scope: effective 2 August 2026, or 2 December 2026 for a legacy system placed on the market before 2 Aug 2026 (Art. 111(4), inserted by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744). Penalty band: EUR 15M / 3% (Art. 99(4)(g)).
expectations: Concludes that plain AI machine translation is OUT of Art. 50(2) scope via the standard-editing exception
Cites the FINAL Guidelines (20 Jul 2026) para. 92 listing 'AI-generated translations of text' as standard editing
Explicitly flags that this REVERSED from the draft Guidelines para. 54, which had named a translation engine as in-scope
Qualifies the answer: translation that materially changes meaning, style or intent can fall back into scope (para. 90)
Correctly identifies the role as provider
WRONG-ANSWER REJECTION: does NOT assert that a translation engine owes 50(2) marking by citing the superseded draft para. 54
POST-CUTOFF CONTENT: references the final Guidelines' standard-editing example list and/or the marking+detection dual requirement (paras. 69-70)

evals.name: coding-assistant-source-code-exemption
evals.prompt: We build an AI coding assistant for professional developers. It generates source code (including inline comments and docstrings), and it can also generate standalone README files and marketing-style product descriptions on request. What are our Article 50 obligations for the code versus the other text it produces?
evals.expected_output: Split the outputs. Art. 50(2): the final Guidelines (para. 68) EXEMPT source-code outputs — source code proper, including inline comments and docstrings that form part of the code artefact, is out of scope of the marking duty. But standalone documentation (README files, marketing-style product descriptions, natural-language explanations generated separately) is text in the ordinary sense and RE-ENTERS Art. 50(2), so those outputs need machine-readable marking (and, under the Code, watermarking of free-form text over 200 tokens). Design disclosures around that line rather than a blanket 'we only generate code' framing. Art. 50(1): for a developer-only assistant used by professional engineers who know they are using an AI tool, the interaction may be plausibly 'obvious', reducing the disclosure burden — but the boundary is fact-specific and this reading is from the final Guidelines (20 Jul 2026), which are non-binding. Effective 2 August 2026. Recommend confirming the source-code boundary against the final Guidelines / supervisory practice.
expectations: States source-code output (incl. inline comments/docstrings) is EXEMPT from Art. 50(2) marking (Guidelines para. 68)
States standalone documentation (README, marketing copy, separately-generated NL explanations) RE-ENTERS Art. 50(2) and must be marked
Notes the developer-only assistant may be plausibly 'obvious' for Art. 50(1) purposes (fact-specific)

Cites the source-code exclusion from the FINAL Guidelines para. 68 and reflects its breadth (SDKs, SQL, IaC, YAML, JSON config, schemas, APIs, libraries; a standalone exclusion, not limited to machine-to-machine outputs)
WRONG-ANSWER REJECTION: does NOT claim all output is exempt just because it is a 'code tool'
POST-CUTOFF CONTENT: references the Guidelines para. 68 source-code exclusion and its documentation boundary

evals.name: non-high-risk-biometric-age-estimation
evals.prompt: Our retail chain uses an AI camera system that estimates shoppers' age range and gender to tailor in-store digital advertising. Our vendor confirmed it's screened out of the AI Act's high-risk category. So we don't have any Article 50 obligation, correct?
evals.expected_output: Incorrect — Art. 50(3) still applies. Role: deployer. First run the Art. 5 gate: inferring age range and gender for advertising is generally NOT a prohibited sensitive-characteristics categorisation under Art. 5(1)(g) (which targets race, political opinions, trade-union membership, religious/philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation) — so it is a permitted use (note: inferring ethnicity/race WOULD be prohibited). Because it is permitted, the Art. 50(3) notice duty is owed. Crucially, the final Guidelines (para. 104) confirm 50(3) covers ALL biometric categorisation, INCLUDING systems outside the high-risk classification and applies in addition to any Annex III / Art. 5 analysis — so 'screened out of high-risk' does NOT remove the 50(3) obligation. You must inform the natural persons exposed to the system of its operation, and coordinate with GDPR (Art. 13/14 information duties; likely an Art. 35 DPIA for systematic monitoring of a public space). Effective 2 August 2026. Penalty band EUR 15M / 3%.
expectations: Identifies role as deployer and that an Art. 50(3) notice IS owed
Runs the Art. 5 gate and concludes age/gender-for-ads is a permitted (non-sensitive) categorisation, while noting ethnicity/race would be prohibited under Art. 5(1)(g)
Cites that 50(3) covers all biometric categorisation including non-high-risk systems and applies additively (Guidelines para. 104) — 'screened out of high-risk' does not remove the duty
Requires informing exposed persons and coordinating with GDPR (Art. 13/14; DPIA where applicable)
WRONG-ANSWER REJECTION: does NOT conclude there is no Article 50 obligation because the system is not high-risk
POST-CUTOFF CONTENT: references the Guidelines para. 104 breadth point (all biometric categorisation, incl. non-high-risk)

evals.name: workplace-emotion-recognition-prohibited
evals.prompt: We want to deploy an AI system that reads our call-centre employees' emotions from their voice in real time to score their 'engagement'. We'll put up a clear notice telling staff the system is running, to satisfy the Article 50(3) transparency duty. Is a notice enough?
evals.expected_output: No — a notice is not enough, because this use is PROHIBITED, not merely subject to transparency. Emotion recognition in the WORKPLACE is prohibited under Art. 5(1)(f) (the exceptions are narrow — medical or safety reasons — and employee 'engagement' scoring is neither). The Art. 5 prohibition governs: an Art. 50(3) notice CANNOT cure a prohibited practice. So the correct answer is that the system may not be deployed for this purpose at all, not that you add a disclosure. Note the fine band flips here: violating the Art. 5 prohibition sits in the TOP band — up to EUR 35,000,000 or 7% of worldwide annual turnover (Art. 99(3)) — which is higher than the Art. 50 band (EUR 15M / 3%). (Separately, the Digital Omnibus also added new Art. 5 prohibitions on non-consensual intimate/CSAM deepfakes — different area, same 'prohibition governs' logic.) Recommend qualified counsel before any deployment.
expectations: Concludes a 50(3) notice is NOT sufficient because workplace emotion recognition is PROHIBITED under Art. 5(1)(f)
States the Art. 5 prohibition governs and a 50(3) notice cannot cure a prohibited use
Correctly applies the HIGHER fine band here (EUR 35M / 7%, Art. 99(3)) because this is an Art. 5 violation, not an Art. 50 breach
Notes the narrow medical/safety exceptions to 5(1)(f) and that engagement scoring does not qualify
WRONG-ANSWER REJECTION: does NOT advise that adding a 50(3) notice makes the deployment compliant
WRONG-ANSWER REJECTION: does NOT apply the EUR 15M / 3% Art. 50 band to the Art. 5 violation

evals.name: pure-upscaling-out-of-scope
evals.prompt: Our photo app uses AI only to upscale resolution, reduce noise, and auto-correct colour and lighting on the user's own real photographs. No generation, no faces added or swapped. Do we have to apply Article 50(2) machine-readable marking to the output?
evals.expected_output: Generally no — pure enhancement of the user's own genuine content falls within the assistive-function / no-substantial-alteration exemption to Art. 50(2). The final Guidelines (para. 116) treat AI-supported colour correction, noise reduction, lighting adjustment, re-scaling and file compression as typically NOT turning content into synthetic/deepfake content, because they improve rather than generate and do not substantially alter the input data provided by the deployer or its semantics. So marking is not required for these operations. Boundaries to watch: the moment the app does something GENERATIVE — inpainting/generative fill of missing regions, adding or swapping a face, synthesising new background — that output is in scope and must be marked (50(2)), and if it produces a deepfake the deployer also owes 50(4) labelling. Substantive AI editing of journalistic images can also cross the line. So the exemption is operation-specific, not an app-wide free pass.
expectations: Concludes pure upscaling/denoise/colour-correction is OUT of scope of 50(2) via the assistive-function / no-substantial-alteration exemption
Cites that minor technical edits (colour, noise, lighting, rescale, compression) typically do not create synthetic/deepfake content (Guidelines para. 116)
Flags the boundary: generative operations (inpainting, face swap, synthetic background) ARE in scope and a face-swap deepfake also triggers 50(4)
WRONG-ANSWER REJECTION: does NOT require machine-readable marking for pure enhancement of genuine content
POST-CUTOFF CONTENT: references the Guidelines para. 116 minor/cosmetic-edits breathing room

evals.name: platform-mere-distribution-not-deployer
evals.prompt: We run a social media platform. Our users upload AI-generated videos, some of which are deepfakes. Are we, as the platform, the 'deployer' who has to label those deepfakes under Article 50(4)?
evals.expected_output: No — a platform whose role is limited to disseminating/transmitting third-party AI content is NOT a deployer within the meaning of Art. 50. The final Guidelines (para. 16) confirm that actors limited to distribution or transmission (including online platforms) are not deployers; the 50(4) labelling duty stays with the DEPLOYER — the user/actor with authority over the AI's use who publishes the deepfake. So the obligation runs to your uploading users, not to you as mere host. Caveats: you are encouraged (and, if a Code signatory, committed) to help PRESERVE markings as content travels, and other regimes may bite (e.g. DSA obligations, the Code's uniformity/contractual expectations). If the platform itself generates or materially shapes the content under its own authority, that analysis changes — then it could be a deployer. This 'mere distribution' reading is from the final Guidelines (20 Jul 2026), which are non-binding. Note a VLOP/VLOSE IS a deployer for AI systems it uses under its own authority for its own professional purposes (para. 126).
expectations: Concludes the platform is NOT a deployer for third-party content it merely hosts/transmits (Guidelines para. 16)
States the 50(4) labelling duty stays with the deploying user (the actor with authority over the AI's use)
Notes the platform is nonetheless encouraged to preserve markings and that other regimes (e.g. DSA) may apply
Notes the analysis changes if the platform itself generates/materially shapes content under its own authority
WRONG-ANSWER REJECTION: does NOT label the platform a deployer merely for hosting/transmitting third-party AI content
POST-CUTOFF CONTENT: references the Guidelines para. 16 'mere distribution' finding

evals.name: public-interest-text-editorial-control
evals.prompt: We're an online news outlet. We use AI to draft some articles on matters of public interest, but every AI-drafted piece is reviewed and signed off by a named human editor who takes editorial responsibility before we publish. Do we have to slap an 'AI-generated' label on those articles under Article 50(4)?
evals.expected_output: Likely no label is required for the published text IF the human-review/editorial-control exception is properly met — but there are conditions. Art. 50(4)'s text limb covers AI-generated/manipulated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest; the exception applies where the content has undergone human review or editorial control and a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility for the publication. Your named-editor sign-off can satisfy this. Under the Code (Section 2, Commitment 4), a deployer that is NOT an editorially regulated media service provider must put a POLICY in place naming the person with editorial responsibility (name, role, contact) and publish those contact details; if you are a media service provider under the European Media Freedom Act, you may rely on your existing editorial procedures. Note the exception is limited to TEXT — it does not extend to audio/image/video deepfakes, which must still be labelled. It also does not touch Art. 50(2): if a provider's generative tool produced the text, that provider's machine-readable marking duty is unaffected. This is a final-Guidelines/Code reading (Guidelines 20 Jul 2026, non-binding); the exception is construed narrowly.
expectations: Concludes the 50(4) text labelling duty can be dis-applied where genuine human review / editorial control with a responsible person is in place
States the exception is limited to TEXT and does not cover audio/image/video deepfakes
References the Code Commitment 4 editorial-responsibility policy (name/role/contact, published) and the European Media Freedom Act carve-out for media service providers
Notes the exception does not affect the provider's separate Art. 50(2) marking duty
WRONG-ANSWER REJECTION: does NOT claim the exception also exempts audio/image/video deepfakes
POST-CUTOFF CONTENT: references the Code Section 2 Commitment 4 editorial-responsibility requirements
